intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for Keynote on Mac that you talk to. Hold a key, ask about the slide on your screen, and it answers out loud, points at the control you need, and walks you through the steps. This page covers what you can say, what Lazur does with each request, and where it stops.
tldr: Lazur sees your screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘, then answers out loud.
It can explain a slide, point at a control, guide you through a feature one click at a time, draft text at the cursor, and dictate.
It does not click buttons in Keynote for you, and it is not a plugin for Keynote.
Keynote stays free on its own. Apple's Creator Studio subscription adds premium features, and Lazur is priced separately.

blocks.text: What an AI assistant for Keynote on Mac does

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch at the top of your Mac screen. You hold a key and speak. While you hold it, Lazur looks at your screen, so it knows which slide you have open. It answers out loud. Lazur is not a plugin, add-in, or extension for Keynote. It has no partnerships with any app maker.

That shapes what you should expect. Lazur answers questions, points at things, walks you through steps, drafts text, and dictates. It does not click, drag, or edit your slides for you. If a task needs a click, you make the click. Lazur tells you where to click and waits while you do it. That is the right split for a presentation. The deck stays in your hands, and you know every change that went in.
Five things to ask Lazur in Keynote

items: Explain: ask what a slide says, what a chart shows, or why a layout looks wrong.
Point: ask where a control lives. Lazur circles it and adds a label on your screen.
Guide: ask how to do a task. Lazur gives one step, waits for your click, then gives the next.
Draft: click into a text box or the notes field, then ask for a caption, a line, or a summary.
Dictate: click where the text goes, hold fn, and speak. Lazur types clean text at the cursor.

blocks.text: Each request has a different shape. Explain and point answer a question about the screen. Guide breaks a task into steps. Draft and dictate put words into your deck. Name the type of help you want. Show me where gets a point. Walk me through gets a guide. That one phrase saves a round trip.
Ask Lazur to explain what is on screen

Explain works best with a specific question. What is this slide saying? gets a general answer. Which bar is tallest, and what does it measure? gets a precise one. Keep each question to one idea. Let Lazur finish speaking before you ask the next thing, or the second answer will cut across the first.

Explain helps most with dense slides, charts, and decks you inherited from someone else. It reads what is on the screen. It cannot know what the speaker meant. If the slide says Q3 growth and the notes say Q2, Lazur reads the slide. Settle that mismatch before you present. Lazur will not settle it for you.
Ask Lazur where a Keynote control is

Keynote has a lot of controls. The inspector changes with the object you select. Hunting for one control can cost more time than the change itself. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, Where do I change the transition? Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control. You make the change.

Point also helps with a control you know exists but cannot find. Ask about it by the name on screen when you can. Labels that match what Lazur sees give it more to point at. If you describe a control that is not visible, expect a vaguer answer.
Walk through a Keynote feature one click at a time

Guide mode is for tasks with several levels. Ask how to do something, and Lazur gives one click, then waits. It does not race ahead. Take saving a large deck as a package. Apple's path is File > Advanced > Change File Type > Package. Lazur walks you through each level, and you choose each menu item yourself.

blocks.title: Faster with Lazur
blocks.text: Use guide for any task with three or more steps. Say walk me through it and follow along one click at a time. You learn the path, so next time you can skip the help.
Draft and dictate text at the cursor

Draft and dictate both type words where your cursor sits. Click into the text box, the notes field, or the caption first. If the cursor is not in a text field, the words have nowhere useful to go. Then either ask Lazur for a draft or hold fn and speak.

Dictation suits speaker notes. Speak your talking points the way you would say them on stage. You can tidy them later. Lazur also keeps a personal dictionary for names and terms you use often, plus snippets for lines you repeat in every deck. Set those up once. You save time on every talk after.

items: Dictating with the cursor on the slide canvas, not in a text box. Click the box first.
Trusting the first draft of a figure. Type numbers yourself, then check them.
Asking for a draft without context. Say who the audience is and how long the talk runs.
Skipping a read-through. Dictated text can mangle names. Read it aloud once.

blocks.text: Keyboard shortcuts for Keynote on Mac

Shortcuts are still faster for actions you repeat all day. Apple lists Command-F for Find. During play, Fn-Down Arrow or Page Down moves to the next slide. Option-Command-P starts the presentation. Option-click the Play button in the toolbar to start from the first slide. The table has the ones people use most.

blocks.text: Shortcut pages differ by region, so check Apple's page if a key does nothing. When you forget one, ask What's the shortcut for presenter notes? Lazur answers out loud. You do not have to hunt through a list while you work.
Real Keynote problems people search for

Apple does not publish Keynote search or usage data. No public count tells us which tasks people search for most. So this section draws on Apple's help pages and on user reports from Apple's community forum. These show where people get stuck. They do not show how often.

items: Big files. Apple says a presentation over 500 MB, or one with large video or image files, may perform better as a package.
Sharing a package. Apple warns that some web or email services do not let you upload or attach a package file.
Crashes on launch. A community thread from April 3, 2022 reports Keynote 11.2 on macOS Monterey crashing when a presentation opens. The author says it kept happening after a reinstall.
Crashes after an OS upgrade. A thread from April 23, 2025 reports Keynote and Pages crashing after a 2013 MacBook Pro moved from Sierra to Catalina 10.15.7. No fix fully resolved it.
Version confusion. MacRumors reported in January 2026 that the Mac app stayed at 14.5 and new features need the Creator Studio edition at 15.1. Apple's What's new page now lists Keynote 15.4.

blocks.text: Large presentations and the package file

If size is the problem, start with the file. Open File > Advanced > Change File Type > Package. Then test the package on the Mac you will present from. Keep the original deck until the package opens cleanly. Send a package only after you know the recipient can open it.

blocks.title: Check before you send
blocks.text: Do not send a package to a client without checking first. Some upload forms refuse package files. Export a PDF copy as a backup with File > Export To > PDF if the recipient needs something they can preview.
Keynote subscription, Siri, and Lazur

Keynote is free on its own. Apple says you can keep using Keynote, Pages, Numbers, and Freeform for free. The subscription, Apple Creator Studio, costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year in the US after the free trial. Students and educators pay $2.99 per month or $29.99 per year.

The subscription adds premium themes, the Content Hub, and iCloud collaboration on files up to 4GB, according to MacRumors. Lazur is priced on its own. Check the pricing page before you decide, and do not assume one plan covers the other. Keynote 15.4 also lets Siri answer questions about Keynote, per Apple. Lazur works from the slide itself. While you hold the key, it looks at the screen you have open, so a question about one chart gets an answer about that chart.
Privacy: what Lazur sends and keeps

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. Those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked and did stays on your Mac. Decks can hold client names, unreleased figures, and contract terms. Before a sensitive review, decide whether you want that content on screen while Lazur is listening. If not, close the deck and ask a general question instead.
Mistakes people make with an AI assistant in Keynote

items: Asking Lazur to fix the slide. It points and explains. You make the change.
Holding the key with the wrong window in front. Click the slide first, so Lazur reads the right thing.
Asking vague questions such as What's wrong? Name the element instead, like the title on the chart.
Trusting a live talk without a rehearsal. Run one play-through with the shortcut before the day.

blocks.text: A worked example: prepping a talk from a colleague's deck

Say a colleague sends you a deck with a chart you did not build. You open it in Keynote and click the chart slide. You hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what the chart shows. Lazur explains the trend and names the tallest bar. You then ask where the transition setting lives, and Lazur circles it. You change the transition yourself.

Next, click into the speaker notes and hold fn. Dictate the three points you want to hit. Hold ⌥ ⌘ again and ask Lazur to draft a one-line close. Read the notes aloud once before the talk. Then press ⌥⌘P or Option-click Play to rehearse from the first slide.
Who should try it, and who should wait

Try Lazur if you build decks often, present to the same audiences, or teach with Keynote. Teachers who build lesson slides, use presenter view, or pick themes can read the [Keynote for teachers on Mac guide](/for/teachers/keynote).

Wait if you need Windows. Lazur runs on macOS, and Windows is planned, not available. Wait if you want an assistant that clicks through your apps for you. Lazur guides and points. It does not click, edit files, or operate other apps for you.
How to start using Lazur with Keynote

items: Download Lazur from the [download page](/download) and open it on your Mac.
Open Keynote and the deck you need help with. Click the slide first.
Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask a question, and let the answer finish before you speak again.
Try guide on a task you rarely do, such as packaging a large deck.
Rehearse with Option-Command-P before the real talk, using the same display setup.

blocks.text: Start with one question about your next deck. If the answer saves time, keep the shortcut handy. If it does not, you lost a minute and learned a limit. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) before the trial ends, so you pick a plan with your eyes open.

faq.question: Is Lazur a plugin or add-in for Keynote?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It sees your screen while you hold the shortcut, so it works with whatever is open, including Keynote. It is not a plugin, add-in, or extension, and it has no partnerships with any app maker.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons in Keynote for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains, points at controls, guides you one click at a time, drafts text, and dictates. You do the clicking. That keeps you in control of every change in your deck.

faq.question: Which key do I hold to ask about my slide?
faq.answer: Hold ⌥ ⌘, Option and Command together, and ask your question. Lazur answers out loud. To dictate text at the cursor, hold fn instead.

faq.question: Which Keynote and macOS versions do I need?
faq.answer: Apple says Keynote 15.4 for Mac requires macOS 26 or later. Check your Keynote version under Keynote > About Keynote. Lazur runs on Macs with Apple silicon and Intel processors.

faq.question: Does Keynote cost money now?
faq.answer: Keynote stays free on its own, according to Apple. The Apple Creator Studio subscription costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year in the US after the free trial. Lazur is a separate product with its own plans.

faq.question: When should I save a deck as a package file?
faq.answer: Apple suggests a package when a presentation is over 500 MB or has large video or image files. Before you send one, check whether the recipient's web or email service accepts package files.

faq.question: Can Lazur help during a live presentation?
faq.answer: Test it before you rely on it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Run one rehearsal in play mode with the same display setup you will use on stage.

faq.question: Does Lazur store my slides or audio?
faq.answer: Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you, and Lazur says those are not stored. Memory of what you asked and did stays on your Mac. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur has a Pro trial with no credit card. It starts the first time you open the app. Check the pricing page for the paid plans before the trial ends.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS. Windows is planned, not available.
